lesson_title: Trust and Distributed Systems: Foundations for Blockchain

questions.question_stem: A wallet service depends on a hosted API to report balances accurately. In an engineering sense, what is the system doing?
questions.correct_answer: It is making an explicit trust assumption about the hosted API's behavior.
incorrect_answers: It is avoiding trust because an API response is only a technical interface.
It verifies balances independently because the hosted API response uses HTTPS.
It distributes trust because many wallets query the same hosted API endpoint.
questions.explanation: The lesson defines trust as a concrete dependency on some entity behaving as expected, not as a feeling of personal confidence.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/introduction_05-IN-trust_and_distributed_systems_foundations_for_blockchain-slides-only.qmd: Trust; What is trust in digital systems?

questions.question_stem: A payment network removes its central database and lets peers maintain replicated state under shared rules. Which tradeoff best characterizes this architectural shift?
questions.correct_answer: It reduces reliance on one central authority but increases coordination and verification complexity.
incorrect_answers: It eliminates institutional trust by treating each peer replica as authoritative in practice.
It reduces coordination work because each replica only checks nearby peer updates before syncing.
It shifts the single point of failure to the peer that first receives each transaction request.
questions.explanation: Distributed architectures relocate trust into mechanisms such as cryptography, consensus rules, and peer assumptions; they do not remove the need for trust or coordination.

questions.question_stem: In a mutually suspicious network, a peer receives a transaction claim from another peer. What response best reflects the correct design posture?
questions.correct_answer: Verify the claim against protocol rules before relying on it.
incorrect_answers: Weight the claim by sender reputation before applying local checks.
Quarantine the claim until a central operator approves the sender.
Forward the claim so peer consensus runs before local validation.
questions.explanation: Mutual suspicion means participants are designed to verify behavior rather than assume that other participants are benign or correct.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/introduction_05-IN-trust_and_distributed_systems_foundations_for_blockchain-slides-only.qmd: Why Suspicion Matters; Suspicion In Practice

questions.question_stem: A node stays online and replies promptly, but it returns corrupted account data while claiming the data is valid. Which fault type does this best illustrate?
incorrect_answers: Omission faults
Crash-stop fault
Late timing fault
questions.explanation: A commission fault involves an active node returning incorrect data. It is more serious than simply going silent, dropping a message, or replying late.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/introduction_05-IN-trust_and_distributed_systems_foundations_for_blockchain-slides-only.qmd: Crash Faults / Omission Faults / Timing Faults / Commission Faults

questions.question_stem: A peer sends one version of the ledger tip to some neighbors and a conflicting version to others, adapting its lies as it observes responses. Which fault model is the best fit?
incorrect_answers: Crash-stop fault
Late timing bug
Omission fault
questions.explanation: Byzantine faults include arbitrary, malicious, and adaptive behavior, especially active deception that can create inconsistent views across honest nodes.

questions.question_stem: Why is a crash fault usually easier to handle than Byzantine behavior?
questions.correct_answer: A crashed node stops responding, while a Byzantine node may remain active and mislead different peers in different ways.
incorrect_answers: A crashed node usually means its stored data is wrong, while Byzantine behavior mostly means messages arrive late.
A crashed node can be handled by trusting its last known state, while Byzantine behavior only needs duplicate paths.
A crashed node creates conflicting reports for peers, while Byzantine behavior is limited to one visible outage.
questions.explanation: Simple redundancy and timeouts can often handle silence. Active deception is harder because the node still participates and can manipulate honest participants' local views.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/introduction_05-IN-trust_and_distributed_systems_foundations_for_blockchain-slides-only.qmd: Crash Faults / Omission Faults / Timing Faults / Commission Faults; Byzantine Faults

questions.question_stem: A network sees several nodes stop responding. Operators cannot tell whether hardware failed, packets are being dropped, or an attacker is causing a denial-of-service condition. What concept explains why the defense should focus on observable behavior?
incorrect_answers: Timing fault model
Fault threshold rule
Classical consensus
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that benign faults and malicious attacks can look the same from a node's perspective, so systems must defend against behaviors rather than wait to prove intent.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/introduction_05-IN-trust_and_distributed_systems_foundations_for_blockchain-slides-only.qmd: The Ambiguity of Intent; Why Failures Become Security Risks

questions.question_stem: A consensus protocol keeps accepting new transactions, but two groups of honest nodes finalize conflicting histories. Which consensus goal has been violated most directly?
incorrect_answers: Liveness (progress)
Throughput (capacity)
Identity trust model
questions.explanation: Safety is the requirement that the system not contradict itself by allowing honest participants to settle on inconsistent states.

questions.question_stem: A consensus protocol never finalizes conflicting histories, but it stops confirming new transactions indefinitely after a network disruption. Which goal is failing?
incorrect_answers: Safety state agreement
Validity condition check
Authentication rule set
questions.explanation: Liveness is the requirement that the system continue making progress. A stalled but non-contradictory protocol preserves safety while losing liveness.

questions.question_stem: Why can simple majority voting break down in the Byzantine Generals Problem?
questions.correct_answer: A traitor can give different honest participants different evidence, so they may each compute a majority over different inputs.
incorrect_answers: Majority voting fails because honest participants are required to ignore relayed reports and use only direct messages from the sender.
The issue is that honest participants use different majority rules, so one shared tie breaker would restore agreement.
Oral messages make reports publicly verifiable, so conflicting inputs are discarded before any majority vote begins.
questions.explanation: The core challenge is not voting itself but ensuring honest participants share a consistent view before applying a decision rule.

questions.question_stem: What contrast do classical protocols such as two-phase commit, Paxos, and Raft illustrate when compared with blockchain consensus?
questions.correct_answer: Benign crash or omission faults are easier to address than open adversarial Byzantine behavior.
incorrect_answers: Replicated databases can skip adversary assumptions because leader election prevents lying nodes.
Public blockchains mainly solve routine crash recovery rather than malicious equivocation.
Once replicas use quorums, the difference between benign and malicious faults disappears.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses classical consensus to show that distributed systems had tools for benign environments, while blockchains face harder open-network adversaries.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/introduction_05-IN-trust_and_distributed_systems_foundations_for_blockchain-slides-only.qmd: Classical Consensus Approaches; Why Decentralization Is Harder

questions.question_stem: A designer says a blockchain removes trust because users no longer rely on a bank. Which response is correct?
questions.correct_answer: The system has relocated trust into cryptographic proofs, consensus rules, and assumptions about enough honest participation.
incorrect_answers: The system eliminates trust because a valid signature is enough to make any proposed ledger state correct by itself.
The system shifts trust from the bank to whichever peer reports the newest transaction history to each user first.
The system avoids trust by letting users download records while preventing them from checking consensus rules directly.
questions.explanation: The visible slides frame trust in digital systems as explicit assumptions and dependencies. Distributed architectures shift trust away from a central institution toward cryptographic proofs, consensus rules, and participant behavior assumptions.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/introduction_05-IN-trust_and_distributed_systems_foundations_for_blockchain-slides-only.qmd: What is trust in digital systems?; Centralized vs. Distributed Architectures

questions.question_stem: In the interactive consistency framing of Byzantine agreement, what must loyal participants achieve when the source of an input is loyal?
questions.correct_answer: They must agree with one another and use the loyal source's value.
incorrect_answers: They may choose a default even when the original source node is loyal.
They may keep local values as long as a majority vote was computed.
They should prefer the value sent through the shortest network path.
questions.explanation: The reading separates agreement among loyal participants from validity: when the original source is loyal, loyal participants should follow that source's value.

questions.question_stem: An unauthenticated distributed system wants to tolerate one malicious participant using ordinary oral messages. Why is a tiny three-participant design structurally unsafe?
questions.correct_answer: With one traitor, honest participants can be left unable to distinguish which local story is true, so the loyal majority is not large enough.
incorrect_answers: The design is unsafe because oral messages hide sender identity, so honest nodes cannot attribute reported values reliably in the protocol.
The design is unsafe because one missing timeout proves the other participants are malicious and forces a protocol halt before agreement.
The design is unsafe because three participants can form a reliable majority only when signatures are attached to all messages.
questions.explanation: The reading's threshold result for oral messages follows from indistinguishability: to tolerate m traitors, loyal participants must overwhelmingly outnumber the traitors.

questions.question_stem: How do signed messages change the Byzantine agreement problem?
questions.correct_answer: They make a participant's claims transferable and verifiable, limiting forgery and making equivocation visible.
incorrect_answers: They let each participant decide from the first signed value received, without comparing later reports from peers.
They prove the signer is loyal, so honest nodes no longer need to handle conflicting signed orders from that signer.
They remove timeout and connectivity assumptions by treating signed messages as delivered, timely, and unblockable.
questions.explanation: Signed messages do not make consensus trivial, but they constrain what faulty participants can credibly claim and allow honest participants to share evidence.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/reading-05-byzantine.txt: Section 4, A Solution With Signed Messages

questions.question_stem: A protocol declares a message absent after a timeout. What assumption is hidden inside that design choice?
questions.correct_answer: Message delays and clock behavior are bounded well enough for absence to be detectable.
incorrect_answers: The network can identify each sender but makes no bounded claim about delivery time.
Signatures make late messages invalid without a network delay bound or clock assumption.
A majority has already agreed on the missing value before the timeout rule is applied.
questions.explanation: The reading treats timeouts as part of the trusted system model: detecting missing messages depends on bounded delays and sufficiently synchronized clocks.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/reading-05-byzantine.txt: Section 6, Reliable Systems: A3 timeout assumptions
